rv.q: The production is full of pace and creepiness when it could so easily slide into the ridiculous.
This is a brilliant production; I can’t wait for my next visit to the Old Vic, and I will be buying the book tomorrow!
Perhaps Porter’s original manages to balance the mythical with the modern, but in this stage version, there seem to be so many things going on.
Folk horror with an urban twist
Yet there's no avoiding the fact that this Bristol Old Vic production is thin on atmosphere and lacks a much-needed sense of place.
The story survives the journey to the stage. The spell does not.
It’s immediately intriguing, and every creative decision works together to create an environment that feels utterly immersive.

--> “Say your prayers and be good, too, or Dead Papa Toothwort is coming for you.” Rooted in the South West, and with performers from across the region, the play at times veers into the same territory as Jez Butterworth’s Jerusalem . There is a common sense of impending doom firmly rooted in frailties within the human condition.
This is a strikingly imaginative production of a unique book.
But it’s a real shame to see a show with such potential so rarely be given the chance to properly achieve it.
Medina’s production is well-crafted and inventive and, as a team, Bristol Old Vic has risen to the considerable challenge of turning a demanding text into theatrical reality.

But unfortunately these positives are shadowed by a few negatives, from a few poorly written encounters between Lanny and other characters, to the final scene where two separate endings are being formed at once.

cn.t: Critics find this atmospheric adaptation of Max Porter's novel ambitiously imaginative but uneven, with most praising its striking theatricality and folklore elements while some feel the experimental structure doesn't fully cohere.
